doc.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Charlie Parker's compassion and the naming of Ko-Ko
summary: Teddy Reig's story of how Bird renamed Cherokee as Ko-Ko, and Bird's intellect.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Yeah we need food for thought. Boy can we use some of that. That’s true. But I was going to tell you about Charlie Parker.

So I became very curious about this cat, because he was so beautiful as a person. I mean he showed such great compassion and such true concern, beyond all the other musicians that I had met. And I was wondering, this guy, there’s more to him than meets the eye. Then I used to hang out uptown with the songwriters on 50th Street and Broadway. So I ran into Teddy Reig one day. So we got to talking about Bird. Teddy Reig used to sell bass drum beaters. That was his thing that he sold. And he made the first records with Bird and Diz, “Salt Peanuts” and all. So we got to talking about Bird and he says, “man this cat” he says, “when we did ‘Cherokee — ’” [scats] He says, “when we did that, we didn’t have any money and this was the last date so we took it to the publisher to get the license to it and the publisher said it’s a desecration of Ray Noble’s composition and we’re not going to give you the license.” So they couldn’t release the whole thing because they needed that song to complete. Those records they made in those days, they didn’t have any extra songs like they do now. So he says, “oh man,” and they were devastated because they couldn’t get their money back until they put the product out on the market. So he took it to Bird. He says man, what are we going to do? And right away, © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -17-

without any hesitation, Bird says, “change the title, just call it “Ko-Ko.’” He says, “Cocoa, you mean the drink?” He says, “no ‘Ko-Ko.’” And you think that’ll work? Bird says, “why not?” You know the melody isn’t defined anywhere. So they did it, and it was a big hit. And then Teddy Reig says, 20 years later he realized that “Ko-Ko” was the lord high executioner in the mythical kingdom of Titipu in Gilbert & Sullivan’s “The Mikado,” which took place in Mongolia. And Mongolians are the ancestors of all the American Indians and the Eskimos. They walked across the Bering Strait when it was connected. And the ones that stayed up in the north became the Eskimos and the ones that came down in the plains became the Indians. So that Ko-Ko was an ancestor of the Cherokees. Anthropologically. And Bird knew this right away. I said what a mind, what a mind. This guy, it’s amazing, the range of his knowledge. They had a scene in the movie “Bird,” where he goes up to the fenced estate of —

Stravinsky, yeah. Because that was his favorite composer. He was an intellectual, much more than a smoker of reefer or a shoot-up jazz musician, very much more depth to him than that. And this is the part of him that I want to cover. This was a very great man. Far greater than anybody realizes. And you only have to listen to one of his solos to hear the mental agility that inspired Coltrane and everybody else. Brilliant cat.
